hints.quote: It's very important to remember that intellectual disability is a diagnostic condition and not a description.
hints.take: Person-first language: "a patient who has Down syndrome."

hints.quote: Some deficit in intellect, some deficit in ability to adapt, but note the last one: the onset of this would occur during the developmental period, or during childhood.
hints.take: All three parts of the definition, including onset in childhood.

hints.quote: We have an ethical responsibility to get that family connected to a place that can take care of them.
hints.take: The 2018 ADA Code of Ethics: refer, don't just decline.

hints.quote: The point here is not to remember necessarily 280, but just understand that more and more specific genes are being found.
hints.take: Don't memorize the number of ID genes.

hints.quote: Absolutely do not require you to watch this or view it, but if you have time you may find it interesting.
hints.take: The Willowbrook documentary is optional.

hints.quote: I want you to pay special attention to this next sentence: always go into a conversation with a special needs, intellectually disabled patient talking at a normal level, and then back down.
hints.take: Start high, then back down to the social level.

hints.quote: If I stop for their bad behavior, that becomes what's called a contingent escape.
hints.take: Non-contingent escape: the break comes at the goal.

hints.quote: If you're going to have a staff member hold a patient still, that is still a form of physical restraint and requires the same type of consenting that you would do for a papoose board.
hints.take: Active stabilization needs informed consent too.

hints.quote: Consent can be implied or express, so these are two terms to know.
hints.take: Express: words or writing. Implied: conduct.

hints.quote: It is impossible to give informed consent [with] a blanket consent when you're being registered for treatment.
hints.take: Informed consent needs information.

hints.quote: HOMAR is not used at all anymore, and HOME is only really rarely used.
hints.take: Know what they are; don't use them.

hints.quote: Sedation is really beyond the scope of this course.
hints.take: Pharmacologic restraint is outside this course.

hints.quote: This is just absolute cardinal characteristic of Down.
hints.take: Midface hypoplasia.

hints.quote: When it comes to medical history, one of the most important things I need to be thinking about with Down patients are congenital heart diseases.
hints.take: About 50%; AV canal is most common.

hints.quote: The most common dental condition that you're going to see in Down patients is periodontal disease.
hints.take: Early onset, from age 6, faster progression.

hints.quote: I'm repeating myself a lot, but I want you all to get this.
hints.take: Liquid antibiotics: 250 mg/5 mL, 10 mL = 500 mg.

hints.quote: If I have filled this little guy's mouth with water and he can't breathe through his nose, I just cut off his airway.
hints.take: Mouth breathers: water in short bursts.

hints.quote: Anytime that we're involved in a sedation or general anesthesia case with a Down patient, we have to be careful about hyperextending their neck.
hints.take: Atlantoaxial instability, 10-20%.

hints.quote: Of all the slides in this section, this may be my most important slide, and it is dealing with intellectual disability.
hints.take: Most people with CP have normal or near-normal intellect.

hints.quote: I could see something like that popping up on a board somewhere.
hints.take: TORCH: toxoplasmosis, rubella, CMV, herpes.

hints.quote: It is not hypersalivation that's the problem; it is not that their salivary glands are overproducing. It is the dysphagia.
hints.take: Drooling comes from swallowing trouble.

hints.quote: If we restore before the GERD's resolved, then it just gets bad again.
hints.take: Control GERD before restoring asymptomatic erosion.

hints.quote: Always clean it off from the buccal and lingual surfaces, but don't try to take it off of the occlusal table, because it actually protects the occlusal table.
hints.take: G-tube calculus.

hints.quote: Always speak to a CP patient as though they are your peer intellectually.
hints.take: Dysarthria says nothing about cognition.

hints.quote: Probably the most important thing that I wanted to say in this slide on Lesch-Nyhan is it's very difficult to get ourselves to think of extracting perfectly good teeth.
hints.take: Full-mouth extractions may be the best treatment.

hints.quote: Dactyly should always indicate to you that it's dealing with something with fingers or toes.
hints.take: The -dactyly terms.

hints.quote: Airway management is the big issue with them.
hints.take: Pierre Robin sequence.

hints.quote: In general, midface-deficient patients are going to struggle with airway issues.
hints.take: Apert, Down syndrome.

hints.quote: You're not going to remember a lot of these syndromes, but if you've got good resources and quick access, if somebody presents with something you can jump to that.
hints.take: Know how to look them up.

hints.quote: This page comes from Crest's course. It has VERY helpful and practical suggestions that I use regularly.
hints.take: Dr. Mitchell's note on the communication page.

hints.quote: Siblings with Autism: know the rates the three types of siblings experience autism.
hints.take: Identical 77%, fraternal 31%, siblings lower.

hints.quote: It is critical healthcare professionals understand that an autistic child is NOT simply throwing a temper tantrum.
hints.take: Meltdown vs tantrum.

hints.quote: First, a dentist should never attempt treatment on a patient they feel they cannot safely treat. We must refer.
hints.take: Do no harm, then refer.

hints.quote: These are supplemental and not required for the lecture.
hints.take: Ami Klin's full video.

hints.quote: Dietary considerations may be one of the most important preventive measures that we have available to us.
hints.take: Control sugar-sweetened beverages.

hints.quote: When you see this type of tissue manifestation, make certain that you check under the margins for the presence of calculus.
hints.take: Swollen gingiva hides a calculus ring.

hints.quote: Please don't prescribe it to anyone who's under eight years of age.
hints.take: Home fluoride rinses and gels: 8 and up.

hints.quote: A good diagnostic question across the board is: in a typical day, what does the patient drink the most?
hints.take: The diet question.

hints.quote: Take prevention seriously. If we can prevent disease, we can make things so much better.
hints.take: Prevention is the most important thing we do for them.

hints.quote: Each section does a really nice job about talking about the dental issues and what to expect if you have a patient that is facing some of these issues, so I ask that you spend some time looking at that.
hints.take: Focus on each disorder's dental implications.

hints.quote: Mental health is actually not an area that I consider myself an expert in.
hints.take: The reading, not a lecture, is the source.

intro: ID = intellectual + adaptive deficits + onset in the developmental period (DSM-5)
Old test: IQ under 70; now a long clinical evaluation, with culture and language
Feeble-minded (moron 7-12, imbecile 2-7, idiot under 2) → mental retardation → Rosa's Law 2010 → DSM-5 2013
A diagnosis, not a description: "a patient who has Down syndrome"
Institutions → Willowbrook (Geraldo Rivera) → deinstitutionalization (1970s); special ed by 1978
Most live at home; group homes 6-8 clients; institutions 1-2% (Glenwood)
Any disability: 1 in 5 U.S., 1 in 3 Alabama. Severe: 12.6% U.S., 16.7% Alabama, West Virginia 19.4%
No cause in 30-40%; FAS 2%; ACEs: dose-related, cortisol, hippocampus, 15x suicide
CODA 2019: assessing AND managing; ADA 2018: disability added, so refer
behavior: Maladaptive behavior: can't adapt to the dental setting (a subset only)
Limits on care: ability to benefit and ability to tolerate
Communication is the least invasive tool; tone carries even without words
Social age; start normal, then back down
Clear goals: what I do, what you do, how long
Non-contingent escape: finish the goal, then the break; stopping for behavior = contingent escape
Water in short bursts; 45 degrees; lights off; fewer people; same room and staff
Active = person, passive = device; both need informed consent
Least restrictive, least injurious; never punishment or convenience; not using it can be negligence
Molt prop on posterior teeth; fingers in the vestibule; no HOME/HOMAR
Papoose = brand; Rainbow Wrap has a hinge; X over the chest
Express (words/writing) vs implied (conduct); capacity + information + voluntary
No consent: assault and battery, malpractice. Document justification
Competent patients can refuse; beneficence otherwise; advocate
down: ID: 42% mild, 26% moderate, 15% severe, 17% profound; Alzheimer's changes in 100% of autopsies
Happy, loving, sensitive to mood; worse behavior as ID increases
Midface hypoplasia (cardinal), saddle nose, low ears, epicanthal folds: mouth breathers
Heart ~50%: AV canal most common; tetralogy needs prophylaxis; MVP 57% on EKG
Leukemia 15-50x; pneumonia killed before antibiotics; thyroid, diabetes 3x, celiac 20%
Sleep apnea 50-80%, dysphagia 58%, GERD 60%; atlantoaxial instability 10-20%: don't hyperextend
Class III (small maxilla), crossbite 71%, macroglossia, missing laterals 35-43%, taurodontism
Perio is #1: early onset 60-95%, from age 6; NUG 45% without pain
Strong over esthetic as ID increases
cp: Permanent, non-progressive disorder of voluntary movement and posture
1 in 303; risk rises as birth weight and gestation fall
Prenatal 70-80% (TORCH, multiples), neonatal 10-28% (hypoxia is a small share), postnatal 5-18%
Spastic 70-80% cortex; dyskinetic 10-20% basal ganglia; ataxic 5-10% cerebellum
Most have normal or near-normal intellect: never assume ID from speech
Epilepsy 30%: Stop, Remove, Side, Safe, Allow, Release; >5 min = status epilepticus, EMS
Dilantin hyperplasia; Depakote bleeding; bisphosphonates osteonecrosis
Dysphagia: sit up, short water bursts; GERD >50%: scooped erosion, restore after GERD control
Drooling 10-40% is dysphagia, not hypersalivation; drying the mouth is a last resort
Dysarthria 88%; most consent themselves and can refuse
Long face, open bite, flared incisors, Class II; trauma risk
Perio 3x without extra calculus; g-tube: leave occlusal calculus
Bruxism 58%, pulp exposures rare; tooth number, eruption and tongue normal
Fat or long handles; no Waterpik, disclosing tablets or rinses; lock wheelchair wheels, 45 degrees
syndromes: -dactyly: brachy short, syn fused, clino bent, ectro missing, poly extra
Coloboma hole in iris; miosis small, mydriasis big; hypertelorism wide-set eyes
Glossoptosis: tongue down and back: cleft palate, airway
Scoliosis sideways (C or S), kyphosis backward: pillows
Fragile X: FMR1 repeats, boys, long face, prominent jaw, autistic behaviors
Prader-Willi: paternal 15q deleted; appetite, obesity, outbursts, pain insensitivity; thick saliva → calculus
Tuberous sclerosis: benign tumors; findings depend on location
Apert: craniosynostosis, syndactyly, midface deficiency, crowding, Class III, open bite
Lesch-Nyhan: HPRT1, uric acid, males, self-biting: full-mouth extractions may be right
Pierre Robin: micrognathia, glossoptosis, U-shaped cleft; normal intellect; airway
FAS: smooth philtrum, thin upper lip; mild to moderate
Cornelia de Lange: thick eyebrows, moderate-severe ID, spaced microdont teeth, combative
autism: CDC: developmental disabilities with social, communication and behavioral challenges
Twins: identical 77%, fraternal 31%; ~25% single gene, often de novo; 200-400 genes
Before age 3; no name response 12 mo, no pointing 14 mo, no pretend 18 mo
Stimming: leave it unless it disrupts; then redirect
Meltdown ≠ tantrum: learn triggers and warning signs
Sensory defensiveness: x-ray vest, sunglasses, warnings, firm touch
More caries, attrition, erosion, trauma; no physical tooth differences
Practice kit; first appointment of the day; lights low, sterilizers off
Literal language, "hands on belly", say once and wait, calm praise, no "can I?"
Lying down, midline first, count to 10
Oral sedation mild; IV needs a license; adult OR access scarce; refer
prevention: Varnish only at Sparks: no tray, stronger, eat right away
ADA: sealant + varnish 67/100 occlusal; varnish 46/100 approximal; Prevident 5000 for root caries
SDF small lesions; RMGI releases fluoride; steel crowns for big ones
Swollen gingiva = check under the margin for a calculus ring
Lower lip blocks the brush: pull it down
Rubber cup at the margin, roll interproximal, pulse for gaggers
Surround brush, fat or long handles, 90-degree flosser, sonic brushes
Positions: standing (least gag) → floor with two (most control, most gag)
No home fluoride rinses or gels under 8; consider contact time
Prevident at night, no rinse; GelKam stannous; MI Paste Plus has fluoride
Ask: what does he drink most? Water, plain milk, unsweet tea; ≤10 calories per serving is safe
mental: Mental illness (psychiatric, may come and go) vs ID (cognitive, permanent); 17% vs 3%
Depression: neglect, rampant decay, perio, xerostomia (Prozac 14%, tricyclics 45%)
Tricyclics: epinephrine with prudence, no levonordefrin or norepinephrine; MAOIs: no meperidine
ECT: mouth guard; fix loose teeth and prostheses first
Bipolar mania: over-brushing abrasion; lithium: xerostomia, stomatitis; NSAIDs raise lithium
Schizophrenia: approach slowly; antipsychotics → EPS, tardive dyskinesia, akathisia; careful with sedatives
Dementia: treat early, radiographs early; elderly: 2x peak and half-life; nouns, not pronouns
Alcohol: bleeding profile, cross-tolerance, oral cancer, Antabuse = no alcohol mouthwash
Recovering: no nitrous or mood-altering drugs; NSAIDs, bupivacaine

A staff member's hold is restraint too: active stabilization needs informed consent
Implied vs express consent; a blanket consent is not informed consent

Behavior support: least invasive first; care limited only by the patient's benefit
Protective stabilization done well: when, how, head holds and mouth props
Midface hypoplasia, the cardinal feature: mouth breathing, water and Class III
Congenital heart disease (about half; AV canal) and antibiotic prophylaxis

Pierre Robin sequence: the airway is the big issue

Swollen gingiva: check under the margins for calculus
No take-home fluoride rinses or gels under age 8
Varnish, sealants and SDF: the ADA guideline
Products and contact time: Prevident, GelKam, MI Paste Plus
Home brushing positions and aids
Antidepressants: tricyclics, xerostomia and vasoconstrictors, MAO inhibitors
Bipolar disorder and lithium
